It rings a bell, but it's been a long time.
So the monkeys really like grapes and they tolerate cucumbers. They like cucumbers,
but they like grapes a lot better. And so two monkeys side by side, the researcher
has the one monkey perform a test and gives them a cucumber and it eats it happily. And then the
next monkey, it does the same test and he gives them a grape and they eat it happily. Then with
the first monkey, he goes back and has them do the same thing and hands them a cucumber again,
and they slap it out of his hands.
I was going to say, does he throw it at me?
Like, no, no, no, you gave the other one a grape. I'm not tolerating your stupid cucumber.
That feels very human to me.
That is wild.
Right? That they understand fair, unfair treatment. So that's why I think this is
more about the corruption of creation as well. Now, what happens is when creation is corrupted,
that has a moral significance to us as humans because we're spiritual beings.
So now there's a moral significance. I don't think it's a morally significant thing for
monkeys to do that or for dolphins, as we talked about, the natural world. That was one of our...
I remember that was a Chris Sherrod podcast because he was so fed up that one of our guests
had said something about moral behavior among animals and how they're more moral than we are.
And Chris had said, I'd never looked at that before. We looked it up and he was like,
yeah, they're horrible. The level of abuse and mistreatment by human standards,
they commit against each other. There's nothing about that. The argument just falls flat.
But I think that we see all of creativity created all and the place where it has the
most moral significance is obviously between us and then between us and God.
And that's where there's a moral consequence. And are we guilty of that brokenness? I'm dubious,
although I'm okay if we are because even if that's the case, Christ still offers a way of escape,
which is super generous of him. Are we just corrupted? That I feel confident in. I think
we're corrupted. I think that corruption predisposes us. But I think Adam sinned even
though even if he wasn't corrupted and predisposed, he still sinned and I think I would have too.
So that's kind of my summary of original sin and why I think it's just and appropriate that God
allows it and unpacks it for us. I think I certainly know there have... I have had
opportunities to not sin and I chose to sin. And the minute I've done that ever once in my
entire life, I am guilty. So there you go. Well, thank you so much, Chris. Bryn, thanks for joining
us today. We're rolling with the issues. Yeah, sometimes. But honestly, I'm grateful for more
tackling hard conversations. And it's encouraging to me that we're still getting these questions.
So if you're listening, if you are struggling with anything, please don't hesitate. If you're
close with Chris or me or Bryn or none of us, just shoot us an email. See lechner at southspring.org.
And yeah, this is great. All right. Very good. Great. Thanks, guys.
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Reconstructed Faith. If you enjoyed what you
heard or were challenged, please leave us a review. It'll help other people find us.
If you have questions or a topic you'd like to hear discussed, shoot me an email at info
at southspring.org. Reconstructed Faith is a resource of South Spring Baptist Church.
Remember, don't give up. Trust God. Search for answers.
